idiom_name: ? for error guards, let-else (Rust 1.65) for refutable-pattern guards, if-return as the classic form
implementation_notes: Rust supplies two first-class early exits: ? returns the Err (converted through From) out of the whole function - the book states it returns early and hands the error to the caller - and let-else (stable since 1.65) diverges when a refutable pattern fails, e.g. let Some(x) = ... else { return Err(...) };. Between them they replace most classic if !ok { return ...; } guards, while the plain form remains for failure branches that do more work (logging, mapping a domain error) or where the condition is not itself an error. assert!/debug_assert! mark invariants, and a MutexGuard held by the function is released on any early-exit path, so Rust guards do not need the cleanup discipline the C variant requires.
pitfalls: ? requires the function or closure to return Result/Option; it does not compile in a closure that returns a plain value, and main needs a Result-returning form or a wrapper.
let-else requires the else block to diverge (return, break, panic); an else that continues the happy path is a compile error - restructure the check instead of reaching for unwrap.
let-else needs Rust 1.65+; a crate with an older MSRV keeps if let / match plus return.
